nodes.name: NiO/Ni electrodeposition on Cu foam
nodes.procedure: In order to fabricate a NiO/Ni@Cu self-supporting electrode, the main ingredients used for electrodeposition were copper foam (used as the substrate), NiCl₂ (as the source of Ni), and sodium acetate (serving as a buffering solvent). Fig. 1a schematically depicts the primary fabrication process of the Cu-foam-supported NiO/Ni@Cu electrode using a one-step electrodeposition method.
nodes.source_text: In order to fabricate a NiO/Ni@Cu self-supporting electrode, the main ingredients used for electrodeposition were copper foam (used as the substrate), NiCl₂ (as the source of Ni), and sodium acetate (serving as a buffering solvent).

nodes.evidence_snippet: According to SEM (Fig. 1b–d), the NiO nanosheets are assembled together to form a starfruit structure. There are many metal Ni nanoparticles attached to the 'starfruit'...

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS shows uniform distribution of Ni and O elements.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Meanwhile, the EDS results (Fig. 1e–h) show that the distribution of the Ni and O elements was uniform.

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM shows NiO/Ni heterojunction with d-spacings of 0.209 nm and 0.241 nm for NiO (200) and (111) planes, and 0.176 nm for Ni (200) plane.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The d-spacings of 0.209 and 0.241 nm correspond to the (200) and (111) crystal planes of NiO, respectively, while the d-spacing of 0.176 nm is attributed to the (200) crystal plane of the metal Ni.

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM images show uniform distribution of Ni and O elements.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Moreover, the HAADF-STEM (Fig. 2c–f ) images show that the distribution of the Ni and O elements was uniform.

nodes.characterization_summary: EELS Ni L-edges show chemical valence state of Ni between 0 and +2, with higher oxidation state at P2 indicating mainly NiO.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS, Fig. 2b) shows the Ni L-edges at different positions, which indicates that the chemical valence state of Ni is between 0 and +2.

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD confirms phase composition of NiO/Ni with some Cu substrate signal.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The X-ray diffraction (XRD, Fig. 3a) pattern and Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 3b) further determined the phase compositions of the electrode materials.

nodes.characterization_summary: Raman shows characteristic Ni–O stretching vibration at 527 cm⁻¹ confirming presence of NiO.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 3b, the characteristic signal at 527 cm⁻¹ is assigned to the typical Ni–O stretching vibrations, which confirms the presence of NiO in NiO/Ni@Cu.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni 2p XPS shows peaks at 855.5 eV and 869.5 eV for Ni²⁺ and 852.3 eV and 879.5 eV for Ni⁰; O 1s at 529.3 eV for Ni–O bond.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In the Ni 2p XPS spectra of NiO/Ni@Cu (Fig. 3c), the peaks at 855.5 eV and 869.5 eV with two satellite peaks could be indexed to Ni²⁺, while those at 852.3 eV and 879.5 eV were ascribed to metallic Ni⁰.

nodes.characterization_summary: CV determines double layer capacitance Cdl of 20.03 mF cm⁻² indicating higher ECSA due to starfruit structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Compared to Ni(OH)₂/Ni@Cu (5.87 mF cm⁻²) and Ni@Cu (8.13 mF cm⁻²), NiO/Ni@Cu exhibits a higher Cdl value of 20.03 mF cm⁻², suggesting that the starfruit structure contributes to the exposure of the NiO/Ni@Cu active site.

nodes.characterization_summary: EIS shows charge transfer resistance Rct of 0.4 Ω at 200 mV overpotential.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Nyquist plot of electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) (Fig. 4d) exhibits that the transfer resistance (Rct) of NiO/Ni@Cu is 0.4 Ω...

nodes.characterization_summary: FTIR-ATR shows O–H bending vibration peaks redshifted by 2 cm⁻¹ relative to Ni@Cu, indicating water activation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The bending vibration peaks of the O–H bonds on both NiO/Ni@Cu and Ni(OH)₂/Ni@Cu are redshifted by 2 cm⁻¹ relative to Ni@Cu.
